Item Selection Criteria

All analyses were conducted in R and the anonymised data and analysis code are available on the OSF. For the misinformation items, participants rated each of the 18 candidate statements on two dimensions: the perceived harm of the statement to TGD people from (1) not harmful at all to (4) very harmful and the frequency with which they had encountered it in the media or public discussion from (1) never encountered to (4) frequently encountered. Items were retained on the basis of three criteria: (a) a mean frequency rating at or above the scale midpoint (≥ 2.5) in both subgroups, ensuring retained statements were genuinely encountered; (b) a mean harm rating of at least moderately harmful (≥ 3) in at least one subgroup, a singlesubgroup criterion adopted deliberately to centre the harm judgements of TGD participants rather than requiring both groups to agree; and (c) a face-validity review of near-miss items against their prominence in current UK discourse, which was conducted by LC and BAJ.

For the policy items, participants rated each of the 14 candidate issues for how prominent they currently are in the UK from (1) not at all prominent to (5) extremely prominent.

An issue was retained if it achieved a mean rating at or above the scale midpoint (≥ 3, moderately prominent) in both subgroups, again ensuring cross-community salience rather than relying on the pooled mean.

Results

Misinformation Statements

Ratings for all 18 candidate statements are presented in Table 5. TGD participants rated every statement as both more harmful and more frequently encountered than cisgender participants did. Across both groups, the statements rated most harmful were that "trans women are cisgender men pretending to be women in order to access women's spaces" (item 7; TGD M = 3.72, cisgender M = 3.46) and that "some people identify as trans for predatory reasons" (item 3; TGD M = 3.68, cisgender M = 3.54). The claim that "trans women retain unfair physical advantages in sport" (item 17) was the most frequently encountered in both groups (TGD M = 3.66, cisgender M = 3.38).

Six statements were excluded on the frequency criterion. In each case, TGD participants reported encountering the statement at or above the midpoint, but cisgender participants' mean ratings fell below it (M = 2.16-2.38). These were the claims that "most people who transition later detransition" (item 4), that "children who would otherwise grow up to be gay or lesbian are being pushed towards transition" (item 14), that "there is an organised trans agenda or 'takeover'" (item 9), that "gender-affirming healthcare for young people is experimental" (item 15), that "people become trans because of peer pressure" (item 6), and that "schools are affirming non-human identities" (item 10). All six were rated at least moderately harmful by TGD participants (M = 3.14 -3.48), so their exclusion reflects how rarely cisgender participants reported encountering them rather than a lack of perceived harm. A seventh statement, that "people who accidentally misgender a trans person are likely to be 'cancelled'" (item 8), met the frequency criterion in both groups but fell below the harm threshold in both (TGD M = 2.90, cisgender M = 2.44).

Ten statements met both criteria. Seven of these were rated at least moderately harmful by both groups (items 2, 3, 7, 12, 13, 16 and 18). The remaining three were retained on the basis of TGD participants' harm ratings alone, including the claims that "children are taught about gender identity in inappropriate ways at school" (item 11; TGD M = 3.26, cisgender M = 2.92), that "being trans is a new phenomenon" (item 5; TGD M = 3.22, cisgender M = 2.60), and that "trans women retain unfair advantages in sport" (item 17; TGD M = 3.08, cisgender M = 2.54). One further statement, "Children under the age of 16 are commonly receiving gender-affirming surgeries" (item 1), met the frequency criterion in both groups but fell marginally below the harm threshold in both (TGD M = 2.94, cisgender M = 2.80). It was retained following the face-validity review by the research team, given its prevalence in UK debate. This procedure yielded 11 misinformation items. Note. n = 50 per subgroup. Prominence was rated from 1 (not at all prominent) to 5 (extremely prominent). Issues are ordered by TGD ratings within each section. No. = item number in the ranking survey.

Phase 3: Psychometric Evaluation

The anonymised data, analysis script and materials used in this phase can be found on the OSF (see data availability statement).

Method Participants and Design

To evaluate the psychometric properties of the final misinformation and policy-support measures, we drew on data from two concurrent online cross-sectional surveys hosted on Qualtrics and recruited via Prolific. The first sample comprised 400 self-identifying cisgender participants from the UK, and the second comprised 290 self-identifying TGD participants from the UK, giving a combined sample of 690. Participants overall were aged between 18 and 75 (Mage = 34.52, SDage = 12.10). Cisgender participants (Mage = 39.2, SDage = 12.6) were, on average, older than TGD participants (Mage = 28.1, SDage = 7.7). Wider sample demographics are reported in Table 4. Participants were majority White (87.7%) and based in England (82.9%). During data collection for the cisgender sample, we introduced party-based quotas to offset an emerging skew towards left-leaning participants and better reflect the UK political landscape. No quotas were applied to the TGD sample, which was predominantly left leaning (87.6% left or very left-wing). Collecting data from both groups allowed us to examine the exposure measure in the community the misinformation concerns as well as in the wider public whose attitudes it may shape. The data used in this phase is shared with our companion paper (Cahill et al., under review). However, this paper reports the development and psychometric evaluation of these measures only and does not test the hypotheses preregistered for those studies. There is no overlap in the analyses reported, except for the correlations reported for the discriminant validity check, Materials TGD Misinformation Exposure. This measure comprises the 11 statements retained in the ranking survey (see Table 5). Participants rated how often they had encountered each statement, from 1 (never encountered) to 5 (very frequently encountered). Item responses are averaged, with higher scores indicating greater exposure. The measure was completed by both the cisgender and TGD samples.

TGD Misinformation Agreement.

This measure uses the same 11 statements to assess the extent to which participants endorse each claim. Participants indicated their agreement with each statement from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Item responses are averaged, with higher scores indicating greater endorsement of anti-TGD misinformation.

The measure was completed by the cisgender sample only.

TGD Policy Support.

This measure assesses support for trans-inclusive positions on the four policy issues retained in the ranking survey. Participants indicated their agreement with each statement from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Item responses are averaged, with higher scores indicating greater support for trans-inclusive policies. The measure was completed by the cisgender sample only.

In both surveys, the order of the measures and the order of items within each measure were randomised across participants. Full item wording for all three measures is available in the open materials on the OSF.

Statistical Analysis

All analyses were conducted in R. This phase is a secondary analysis of data collected for a companion study (see Cahill et al., under review). No new data were collected, and the analyses reported here were not pre-registered. The anonymised data and analysis code are available on the OSF. As our sample did not complete all measures, only the exposure measure could be examined in both the cisgender and TGD samples, whereas the agreement and policy items could be examined in the cisgender sample.

The dimensionality of the exposure measure was examined in our sample of cisgender participants (n = 400). Factorability was assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy and Bartlett's test of sphericity. The number of factors to retain was determined by considering parallel analysis, the minimum average partial test, the very simple structure criterion, the eigenvalues and the scree plot together. The resulting structure was then tested by confirmatory factor analysis in the sample of TGD people (n = 290), providing cross-validation in an independent sample drawn from a different population. Model fit was assessed using CFI ≥ .95, TLI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .06 with the 90% CI upper bound ≤ .08, and SRMR ≤ .08.

Measurement invariance of the exposure measure across the two samples was tested using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis, proceeding from configural to loading and intercept equality. Invariance at each step was judged by change in fit, with ΔCFI ≤ .01 and ΔRMSEA ≤ .015 taken to indicate that the added constraints were tenable, rather than by the chi-square difference test alone, which is over-sensitive at this combined sample size. Where a step was not supported, univariate score tests identified the straining constraints, which were released one at a time with the model re-estimated after each. A latent mean comparison between the samples is reported only where partial scalar invariance held with most intercepts constrained.

The agreement items present the same eleven statements with a different response frame and were available in the cisgender sample. Their dimensionality was, therefore, examined by exploratory factor analysis in that sample, using the same retention criteria as above. No confirmatory test is reported.

The four policy support items index support across four distinct contested domains rather than tapping a single underlying construct, and a respondent may reasonably support trans inclusion in one domain but not another. They were treated as a composite index rather than a reflective scale, and internal consistency are reported without factor analysis.

Finally, to examine discriminant validity, we computed Pearson correlations, with 95% confidence intervals, between the exposure, agreement and policy support composites in the cisgender sample. If encountering a claim is distinct from accepting it, exposure should be only modestly associated with agreement, and less strongly associated than agreement with support for trans-inclusive policies.

Results

Item Level Descriptives

Across the full sample, the most frequently encountered claim was that trans women retain unfair physical advantages in sport (M = 4.04), and the least frequently encountered was that children under 16 commonly receive gender-affirming surgeries (M = 2.76). TGD participants reported higher exposure than cisgender participants on every item and higher exposure overall (M = 3.65, SD = .89 and M = 2.93, SD = .87, respectively; t(688) = 10.49, p <.001, Cohen's d = .81, 95% CI = .65 to .97). Notably, this difference was not uniform across items. It was smallest for the sport and prison claims and largest for the grooming and singlesex spaces claims. Standard deviations were comparable across samples and no item showed evidence of a floor effect, though responses to the sport item were concentrated toward the upper end of the scale in both groups.

Agreement with the misinformation statements was assessed in the cisgender sample only (M = 2.80, SD = 1.03). The ordering of agreement broadly followed exposure, with the sport claim attracting the highest agreement (M = 4.05) and the grooming claim the lowest (M = 2.01). Two departures are worth noting. The claims that puberty blockers cause permanent, irreversible harm (M = 3.63) and that trans women retain physical advantages in sport were endorsed more than the frequency of encounter would suggest. In comparison, the claim that trans women are cisgender men seeking access to women's spaces was encountered relatively often but endorsed comparatively rarely (M = 2.27).

Like agreement, support for trans-inclusive policy positions was also assessed using the cisgender sample. Scores were just below the scale midpoint (M = 2.70, SD = 1.22). Support was comparable across three of the four domains (M = 2.84 to 2.96), but markedly lower for participation in competitive sport (M = 2.08). This is the domain whose corresponding misinformation claim was both the most frequently encountered and the most strongly endorsed of the eleven.

Misinformation Exposure and Agreement Factor Analysis

Based on the data from the cisgender sample (n = 400), and prior to conducting the EFA, we examined the skew and kurtosis of each misinformation exposure and agreement item and found all to be within acceptable limits (all <2). The KMO measure was excellent for both the exposure (.94) and agreement items (.95). Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant for both exposure (χ²(55) = 2210.10, p < .001) and agreement (χ²(55) = 2876.12, p < .001), indicating sufficient shared variance among the items to proceed.

For misinformation exposure, the number of factors to retain was examined against the same criteria. The minimum average partial value, the very simple structure criterion, the scree plot and the eigenvalues all indicated a one-factor structure, though parallel analysis suggested two. Given the convergence of the remaining criteria, we proceeded with a one-factor structure.

All eleven items loaded on the retained factor between .54 and .82, and the factor accounted for 49% of the variance. The claim that some people identify as trans for predatory reasons was the best represented (.82), followed by the single-sex spaces claim (.78), while the claim that being trans is a new phenomenon was the weakest (.54). The latter was retained, since its loading exceeded conventional thresholds and the claim is substantively distinct from the remainder of the set.

For misinformation agreement, the number of factors to retain was examined against the same criteria. The minimum average partial value, the very simple structure criterion, the scree plot and the eigenvalues all indicated a one-factor structure, though parallel analysis suggested two. Given the convergence of the remaining criteria, we proceeded with a onefactor structure. All eleven items loaded on the retained factor between .62 and .84, and the factor accounted for 57% of the variance. The claim that children are being taught about trans and gender identity issues inappropriately at school was the best represented (.84), followed by the claims that children and young people transition because it is fashionable and that trans women are cisgender men seeking access to women's spaces (both .82), while the claim that trans women retain unfair physical advantages in sport was the weakest (.62). The latter was retained, since its loading exceeded conventional thresholds, though its comparatively weak association with the remaining items suggests that endorsement of the sport claim is somewhat independent of endorsement of the set as a whole.

Misinformation Exposure Confirmatory Factor Analysis

The one-factor structure was then tested using confirmatory factor analysis with maximum likelihood estimation on the sample of TGD participants (n = 290). The model met all the fit criteria specified above, χ²(44) = 81.26, p = .001, CFI = .979, TLI = .973, RMSEA = .054, 90% CI [.035, .072], SRMR = .031. All eleven items loaded significantly on the factor, with standardised loadings between .65 and .85 and showed the same patterns outlined in the EFA.

Measurement Invariance

Measurement invariance is summarised in Table 7. The configural model met the CFI and SRMR criteria, although RMSEA (.078) exceeded the .06 threshold, reflecting weaker fit of the one-factor model in the cisgender sample. As invariance was evaluated by the change in fit between successive models, we proceeded with the invariance sequence. Constraining the factor loadings to equality produced no meaningful deterioration in fit (ΔCFI = -.002, ΔRMSEA = -.002), indicating that metric invariance held. Constraining the item intercepts produced a substantial deterioration in fit, Δχ²(10) = 106.88, p < .001, ΔCFI = -.025. Full scalar invariance was therefore not supported. Univariate score tests identified four intercepts as responsible: the claims concerning prison placement (χ² = 33.40), competitive sport (χ² = 26.10), grooming by drag performers and trans people (χ² = 21.41), and access to single-sex spaces (χ² = 14.20). The remaining seven fell well below these values. Freeing these four intercepts recovered almost all of the lost fit (CFI = .948, RMSEA = .075, against .951 and .075 for the metric model). Partial scalar invariance therefore held, with seven of the eleven intercepts constrained to equality.

(r = -.78, 95% CI [-.82, -.74]), whereas exposure was only weakly associated with it (r = -.17, 95% CI [-.27, -.08]). This suggests that encountering a claim and accepting it are largely distinct.

Discussion

Research on anti-TGD misinformation has lacked a validated measure of what people actually encounter. Existing instruments capture endorsement of broad belief systems (e.g., Salvati et al., 2024). This conflates encountering a claim with accepting it and means that the measures cannot be applied to the population those claims concern. Our data illustrate the problem directly. Among cisgender participants, exposure and agreement shared less than a tenth of their variance, and agreement, unlike exposure, was closely aligned with policy support, suggesting that endorsement measures sit nearer to attitudes than to what people encounter.

The present research, therefore, provides a measure of exposure to the specific claims currently circulating in the UK, developed with TGD and cisgender participants and evaluated in both populations. The resulting scale is unidimensional, reliable and structurally equivalent across those populations. It is not, however, equivalent in every respect, and these differences may relate primarily to the anti-TGD discourses that exist in the UK. This work also delivers an equivalent measure using the same statements focused on agreement with anti-TGD misinformation and a measure of TGD policy support.

Misinformation Exposure, Agreement and Policy Support Measures

The exposure items formed a single factor in the cisgender sample, with excellent internal consistency, and this structure was confirmed in an independent TGD sample.

Similarly, the same items rated on an agreement scale in the cisgender sample showed the same single-factor structure. The four policy support items were treated as an index of support across distinct domains rather than as a scale, although their internal consistency was also high.

The unidimensionality of the exposure and agreement items is an interesting finding.

Participants who reported encountering one claim tended to report encountering the others, which suggests these claims are not met in isolation but circulate together as a recognisable set. This is consistent with accounts of anti-TGD discourse as a coordinated narrative rather than a collection of separate assertions (Billard, 2023; Connolly et al., 2025), and it supports measuring exposure to a set of claims rather than to any one of them. The pattern of agreement among cisgender participants was less uniform. The claims attracting the strongest endorsement were that "trans women retain unfair physical advantages in sport" and that "puberty blockers cause permanent, irreversible harm", whereas the claim that "drag performers and trans people are grooming children" attracted the weakest. The clearest contrast is between the puberty blockers claim and the claim that "trans women are cisgender men seeking access to women's spaces". Cisgender participants reported encountering both at similar rates, yet endorsed the former far more than the latter, which, like the grooming claim, requires attributing deliberate malice to TGD people. This difference, therefore, does not appear to reflect how often these claims are encountered.

We suggest this may reflect processes identified in research on contemporary expressions of prejudice, though not tested here. Prejudice is more readily expressed where a justification allows them to avoid appearing prejudiced (Crandall & Eshleman, 2003). Widely used justifications also make expressing intolerance seem more socially acceptable. When people encounter these justifications in public, they become significantly more likely to act against minority groups (Bursztyn et al., 2020). Claims framed as empirical questions about fairness or safety provide such a justification, whereas claims requiring the attribution of deliberate harm to children do not and anti-trans rhetoric is characteristically framed as protecting women and children rather than as hostility (Atwood et al., 2024; Billard, 2023; Connolly et al., 2025). If this is correct, anti-TGD misinformation framed in quasi-scientific terms may be more publicly endorsed, and potentially more consequential, than misinformation that is openly hostile. The justification-suppression model of prejudice offers one account of why (Crandall & Eshleman, 2003). People are generally motivated to suppress the expression of prejudice, but express it more readily when a justification is available that allows them to maintain a non-prejudiced self-image. This would also help explain why the policy item that attracted the least support in this sample was the one in which the corresponding claim was the most widely accepted (i.e., participation in competitive sport).

Measurement Invariance

When examining measurement invariance for the misinformation exposure measure specifically, it revealed that while the measure appears to capture the same construct for cisgender and TGD participants, four items were answered differently by both groups at equivalent levels of underlying exposure. Importantly, these differences did not point to TGD participants consistently reporting exposure to claims more frequently. TGD participants reported encountering the single-sex spaces and grooming claims more frequently than their overall level of exposure would predict, and the prison placement and sport claims less frequently. This suggests the pattern is not simply that TGD people encounter more misinformation overall, which the raw item means alone might imply. Three of the four items also refer to trans women specifically, and no other item in the scale does.

Our design cannot provide a definitive reason for these differences, but we present several possible explanations. First, it is possible that claims differ in how they circulate.

Sport and prison placement are prominent in news coverage of policy disputes, reaching both cisgender and TGD populations. However, single-sex spaces and grooming claims may circulate more directly as hostility toward TGD people and, therefore, be more likely to be experienced by TGD people themselves (see: Connolly et al., 2025 for an overview). Second, a claim concerning one's own life may be more memorable than one concerning somebody else's, which would produce a difference in recall rather than in actual encounter (Symons & Johnson, 1997). Third, participants may interpret the response scale differently, in that what counts as encountering something frequently may shift when such content is a constant feature of daily life rather than an occasional news item. Distinguishing between these would require asking participants where they encountered each claim, which we did not do, but this presents an interesting direction for future research.

The Misinformation Climate in the UK

Taken together, each phase offers a description of the current UK misinformation climate that goes beyond the psychometric properties of the measure. In Phase 1, these narratives emerged readily in both the TGD and non-TGD focus groups, with participants recounting claims across domains including predation, safety, and sport. This suggests they are already familiar and circulating in everyday discourse. The claims retained in Phase 2 were those frequently encountered by both groups and judged harmful by at least one. The exposure data from Phase 3 indicate that encounters with them are common in both populations, with most claims reported at or above the midpoint of the scale and the claim concerning sport close to the upper end in both groups. Agreement was also substantial. Among cisgender participants, mean agreement across the eleven claims sat near the scale midpoint, and agreement with the sport claim exceeded four on a five-point scale. Support for trans-inclusive policy was correspondingly low, sitting just below the midpoint overall and markedly lower for participation in competitive sport.

Our companion study examined these relationships directly, and found that exposure was associated with less positive attitudes and lower policy support among cisgender people, operating largely through trans-specific conspiracy beliefs, and with higher mental distress are likely to change. The procedures described in each phase are intended to be reusable for this purpose. All items, scoring instructions, materials and associated analysis files are available on the OSF.

Limitations and future directions

Several limitations should be considered. Most importantly, trans women comprised 16.2% of the TGD sample, while three of the four items showing intercept differences concern trans women specifically. The items that functioned differently across groups therefore concern the group least well represented in the sample used to detect those differences. The underrepresentation of trans women is not unique to this study (see : Cahill et al., 2026), but it has particular relevance here, and future research should seek to oversample this group.

Both samples were predominantly White and based in England, which limits generalisability. The focus groups in Phase 1 were conducted for the purpose of item generation and are not sufficient to support broader thematic claims about how TGD people experience misinformation. The data used in Phase 3 were collected for a companion study rather than for psychometric evaluation, and these analyses were not pre-registered. The agreement items also require confirmation in an independent sample.

The most important omission is that we did not ask participants where they encountered each claim. Without this, the invariance findings can be described but not explained, and the interpretation offered above remains speculative. We suggest that future research qualitatively capture where participants are exposed to relevant misinformation claims as part of any data collection.

The time-bound nature of the items is a feature of the construct rather than a limitation of the measure, although it does mean the present item set should be understood as reflecting a particular moment in UK discourse. The measure is designed to be iteratively updated and expanded on.

Conclusion

This research provides measures of exposure to anti-TGD misinformation, agreement with it, and support for trans-inclusive policy, developed with the communities concerned and evaluated in both cisgender and TGD samples. The claims circulate as a recognisable set rather than in isolation, they are widely encountered and substantially believed. Cisgender and TGD people do not encounter these claims in the same way, and the items on which they differ concern trans women specifically. The measures presented here provide a tool to be used in future research examining misinformation as a minority stress process, or as a predictor of intergroup attitudes and prejudice.

Policy Statements

Prominence ratings for all 14 candidate policy issues are presented in Table 6. The same four issues were rated most prominent by both groups, and all four met the retention criterion.

These issues include single-sex spaces and the Equality Act ruling on the definition of sex (TGD M = 4.48, cisgender M = 3.66), participation of trans people in competitive sport (TGD M = 4.20, cisgender M = 3.82), access to NHS gender services for under-18s (TGD M = 3.92, cisgender M = 3.16), and the placement of trans people in prisons (TGD M = 3.40, cisgender M = 3.08). The two groups ranked these four in the same order, except that cisgender participants rated sport slightly above single-sex spaces.

TGD participants rated a further four issues at or above the midpoint, but cisgender participants did not, including reform of the Gender Recognition Act (TGD M = 3.22, cisgender M = 2.80), school guidance on supporting TGD pupils (3.14 vs 2.90), conversion therapy legislation (3.12 vs 2.68), and access to adult NHS gender services (3.06 vs 2.58). No issue was rated at or above the midpoint by cisgender participants alone. Overall, the issues rated least prominent were census and official data collection on sex and gender identity (TGD M = 2.10, cisgender M = 2.22) and access to social care and community support (TGD M = 2.30, cisgender M = 2.18).

From the four retained issues, the research team developed four directional policysupport items, each worded towards the trans-inclusive position, to operationalise support for trans-inclusive policies. These statements included: 1.

Trans people should be able to access single-sex spaces and services that align with their gender identity.

2. Trans people should be able to participate in competitive sport in line with their gender identity.

Inspection of the freed intercepts indicated that the four differences ran in both directions. TGD participants reported encountering the single-sex spaces claim (3.23 against 3.02) and the grooming claim (2.72 against 2.37) more often than cisgender participants did, and the prison placement claim (2.35 against 2.80) and the sport claim (3.59 against 3.91) less often. Under the partial scalar model, the latent mean of the TGD sample was significantly higher than that of the cisgender sample (Δ = 0.71, SE = .07, p < .001; d = .87), consistent with the observed difference. Note. N = 690 (cisgender: n = 400; TGD: n = 290). ΔCFI and ΔRMSEA for the metric, scalar and partial scalar models are relative to the preceding model in the sequence.

Internal Consistency

Internal consistency was excellent for the misinformation exposure measure in both samples and in the combined sample (cisgender sample: ω = .91, 95% CI [.90, .93]; TGD sample: ω = .92, 95% CI [.91, .94]; combined: ω = .93, 95% CI [.92, .94]). The agreement items, administered in cisgender sample, showed similarly excellent internal consistency (ω = .94, 95% CI [.93, .94]). Although the four policy support items were treated as an index of support across distinct domains rather than as a reflective scale, their internal consistency was also high (ω = .89, 95% CI [.87, .90]).

Discriminant Validity

To examine whether exposure to misinformation is distinct from agreement with it, we examined the correlations between the measures in the cisgender sample. Exposure and agreement were only modestly correlated (r = .29, 95% CI [.20, .38]), sharing less than 10% of their variance. Agreement was strongly associated with support for trans-inclusive policies among TGD people (Cahill et al., under review). The descriptive picture reported here provides the context for those associations. Anti-TGD claims are widely encountered (by both cisgender and TGD people), substantially believed, and associated with low support for the policy positions they concern.

Using the Measures

The exposure measure can be used with both cisgender and TGD samples. Because metric invariance held, associations between exposure and other variables can be compared across the two groups, which is the comparison most research typically desires. Mean comparisons require more caution and should use latent means from a partial scalar model or take account of the four items identified above. We anticipate this measure will be most useful in research treating misinformation exposure as a minority stress process, and in studies assessing media influence on intergroup attitudes and in evaluating interventions intended to reduce the circulation or credibility of such claims. This measure would also be useful in tracking change in the discourse over time.

The agreement measure is intended for use with cisgender samples, where the distinction between encountering and accepting a claim is important. This measure can, and should, be administered alongside the exposure measure, allowing for these two processes to be assessed, which has not previously been possible given existing measures. We would not recommend its use with TGD samples. The policy items assess support across four distinct domains and should be reported separately where sample size permits. These items are likely to be most useful in research on public attitudes toward trans-related policy and in identifying which domains are most contested.

Importantly, these items are time-bound. They reflect the claims circulating in the UK at the time of data collection (Summer 2026). Over time, the prevalence of claims circulating
